title: 10 Disturbing Crimes in Washington History
fullText: Number one, Gary Ridgeway. Once the first body surfaced in the Green River on July 15th, 1982, investigators had less than 8 weeks before four more appeared in the same waterway. The current kept pulling young women downstream, and somewhere behind all of it, a man was going home to his family, eating dinner, watching television, and returning to work at the Kenworth truck plant in Reon the following morning. The gap between these two realities, the expanding body count and the utterly unremarkable life of the man responsible would remain unreached for nearly two decades. By the time technology caught up with Gary Leon Rididgeway, the case file had become the largest serial murder investigation in the history of the United States. Ridgeway was born on February 18th, 1949 in Salt Lake City, Utah. Though the family relocated to the SeaTac area of Washington State when he was still young, he grew up in a home defined by his mother's dominance. Mary Rita Rididgeway was a forceful, controlling woman, and by multiple accounts, young Gary bore the worst of her scrutiny. She publicly humiliated him, dictated his behavior, berated him for bedwedding, a habit that persisted deep into his childhood, and created an atmosphere of shame and suppression around everything relating to bodily function and sexuality. His father, Thomas, was a quieter figure, a bus driver who seemed diminished inside his own home. The dynamic left Gary withdrawn, academically poor, and socially marginal. He tested at an IQ of 82. Teachers had little expectation of him and he had little expectation of himself. What went unspoken and what Ridgeway later disclosed only after his arrest was that even as a young teenager he was developing violent fantasies. He described thoughts of harming his mother. He described arousal linked to control and fear. At the age of 16, he lured a six-year-old boy into the woods near his neighborhood and stabbed him in the liver. The child survived. Ridgeway walked away, apparently telling the boy he had always wanted to know what it felt like to kill someone. This incident was never prosecuted. There is no documented police follow-up. It is one of the most significant missed signals in the entire case. After barely graduating from high school, Rididgeway enlisted in the Navy and was deployed to Vietnam aboard a supply ship. He was not distinguished in service. He married for the first time in 1970 and divorced by 1972. A second marriage followed and ended by 1981. Both former wives later described a man who was obsessed with sex, demanded it constantly, and fluctuated between affection and a cold, remote detachment. Between these marriages, Ridgeway frequented sex workers along the Pacific Highway South corridor, a strip of motel, truck stops, and roadside bars stretching between SeaTac and Tacoma. He learned the landscape, learned the rhythms of the women who worked there, and eventually he stopped paying for what he wanted. The killings likely began in 1982. Ridgeway himself later said he could not remember the exact date his compulsion transitioned from fantasy to action. What is known is that on July 15th, 1982, the body of Wendy Lee Caulfield, age 16, was found strangled and left in the Green River near Kent, Washington. Within the next month, four more bodies were recovered in or near the same waterway. All were young women. Most were connected to the Pacific Highway South corridor. All had been strangled. King County police formed a task force, the Green River Task Force, which would become the longestrunn, most expensive serial murder investigation in the country. At its peak, the task force involved more than 40 investigators, drew consultation from the FBI's newly formed behavioral science unit, and generated a suspect pool numbering in the thousands. And yet, the killings continued. 1983 was catastrophic. Remains were found in clusters, in ravines, behind truck stops, in wooded lots along the highway. Some were discovered within days. Others would not be found for years. Ridgeway deposited bodies in locations he knew well, sometimes returning to interact with them. He later admitted to placing items near the bodies to mislead investigators. Cigarette butts of brands he did not smoke, gum he had not chewed. He also admitted to occasionally placing remains across county lines. Aware that jurisdictional confusion would slow the investigation, Ridgeway's method was manual strangulation, usually from behind, he would approach women along the corridor, offer money or simply a ride, then transport them to a location, often his own home or a nearby wooded area where he would kill them. He sometimes had sexual contact before and after death. He described himself as the best at what he did, a remark chilling in its benality. He said that killing was his career, and the Pacific Highway South was his workplace. What sustained Rididgeway's invisibility was not cleverness, but ordinariness. He did not have the practiced charm of a Ted Bundy, or the social manipulation of other serial offenders. He was quiet, compliant, and forgettable. He showed up for his job at the Kenworth factory, worked on trucks, spoke when spoken to, and went home. He married a third time to Judith Moson in 1988, and by all appearances settled into domestic life. Moson would later say she had no idea. She described a man who was gentle, church-going, and devoted. They read the Bible together. He packed her lunches and at night, sometimes after she was asleep, he would leave the house and go hunting. The investigation came tantalizingly close to identifying him on multiple occasions. In 1983, a sex worker named Marie Malvar's boyfriend saw her get into a pickup truck and followed it to a house, Ridgeway's house. Police questioned Ridgeway. He denied everything. He passed a polygraph test in 1984. He was released in 1987. As DNA profiling began to emerge, investigators obtained a saliva sample from him. The technology at the time was insufficient to produce a match. The sample was stored. Ridgeway was flagged as a suspect, then slowly dropped from active focus as new leads came in and old ones went cold. Through the late 1980s and into the 1990s, the task force shrank, funding was cut, detectives were reassigned. The case entered a kind of institutional limbo, sustained only by the stubbornness of a few investigators, most notably detective Tom Jensen, who refused to let the file close. Meanwhile, Rididgeway continued to kill, though at a slower pace. He later attributed the reduction to his third marriage. He said Judith saved some women's lives by giving him emotional stability. It is a remark that encapsulates the moral void at the center of his psychology. The idea that murder was a default state and love was merely the mechanism that occasionally slowed it. The breakthrough arrived in 2001. Advances in STR DNA analysis allowed the Washington State Patrol Crime Lab to re-examine the 1987 saliva sample. It matched semen recovered from three of the earliest victims. On November 30th, 2001, Ridgeway was arrested at the Kenworth plant, handcuffed in the parking lot, and taken into custody without incident. He showed no visible emotion. The legal proceedings that followed were shaped by a single overriding question. How many more victims were there? Prosecutors in King County struck a plea bargain in exchange for a full confession and the disclosure of all known dumping sites. Ridge Rididgeway would be spared the death penalty. He agreed. Over the course of months, he sat with investigators and methodically recounted murder after murder. He confessed to 49. Detectives believe the actual number exceeds 60. He led them to previously undiscovered remains. He described killings he could not match to specific victims. His memory was detailed in some cases and indifferent in others. He remembered methods. He could not always remember faces. On December 18th, 2003, Ridgeway was sentenced to 48 consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole with a 49th added in 2011. In the courtroom, family members read impact statements. Rididgeway wept, though whether from remorse, self-pity, or some other internal signal, no one could say with certainty. When one father told him he forgave him, Rididgeway broke down entirely. It remains one of the most unsettling moments in American courtroom history. Not because of the forgiveness, but because of the uncertainty about whether the man receiving it had the internal architecture to process it at all. He remains alive as of the last verified reports, incarcerated at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walaw Wala. The Green River investigation fundamentally changed the way serial cases are managed in the United States. It accelerated the integration of DNA technology into law enforcement, reshaped inter agency cooperation protocols, and perhaps most importantly, forced a national reckoning with the reality that the women most targeted by serial predators were also the women most ignored by the systems meant to protect them. The highway corridor where Rididgeway hunted for over a decade was not hidden. It was merely a place most people chose not to see. Number two, Mikuel Anderson. Christmas Eve is supposed to be a night of reunion. Families gather around dinner tables. Children wait for morning gifts and homes fill with warmth that lasts only a few days each year. In Carnation, Washington, the Anderson family expected nothing different. The house on 342nd Avenue Southeast had become the traditional meeting place, where three generations celebrated together every holiday season. There were wrapped presents beneath the tree. There was food prepared for the following morning. Outside, snow covered the quiet streets, muffling every sound in the small farming community. Nothing about that evening suggested it would become one of the darkest crimes in Washington history. By sunrise, six members of the same family would be dead. For several days afterward, no one realized anything was wrong. Friends assumed the family was simply busy with the holidays. Relatives expected delayed phone calls. The children were on winter break, so no absence from school raised immediate concern. It was not until December 26th, 2007 when concerned relatives contacted authorities after repeated unanswered calls that deputies from the King County Sheriff's Office arrived at the Anderson residence. What they discovered inside would shock even veteran homicide investigators. The victims were spread throughout the home. Wayne Anderson, 60, and his wife, Judy Anderson, 58, had been shot to death. Their sons Scott Anderson and his wife Erica had also been executed. Two young children, Olivia, just 5 years old, and Nathan, only three, had been killed as well. The Christmas presents remained unopened. Dinner plates still sat where they had been left. The holiday decorations glowing quietly inside the home created a scene almost impossible for investigators to process. It was less like entering a crime scene and more like walking into a celebration that had been frozen in time by unimaginable violence. There were no signs of forced entry. No evidence suggested strangers had broken into the home. Whoever committed the murders had been welcomed inside. Detectives immediately considered several possibilities. A robbery seemed unlikely because valuables remained untouched. A random attack made even less sense. Carnation was one of the safest communities in Washington, known more for horse farms and quiet neighborhoods than violent crime. The precision of the killings suggested planning familiarity with the house and complete confidence that no one would interrupt. The investigation quickly shifted toward people closest to the victims. Family members were interviewed one after another. friends described Wayne Anderson as hardworking and respected. Judy was known as the emotional center of the family. Scott and Erica were raising two young children while building their future together. By every outward appearance, there were no obvious enemies capable of committing such calculated violence. Then detectives turned their attention to Wayne's daughter, Michelle Anderson. Born in 1971, Mikuel had grown up in the same family now lying dead inside the Carnian home. Those who knew her described a complicated personality. At times, she appeared intelligent and caring. At other moments, she displayed explosive anger, resentment, and an inability to accept responsibility for personal failures. Relationships often deteriorated into conflict. Financial problems followed her throughout adulthood. Arguments with relatives became increasingly common, particularly when money entered the conversation. Her relationship with her parents had grown steadily worse during the years leading up to Christmas 2007. According to investigators, the conflict centered largely on financial support and custody issues involving Mckela's children. Family disagreements had escalated into prolonged disputes that left deep resentment on both sides. While many families argue over money, detectives would later conclude that this resentment had evolved into something far darker. Mikuel was living with her boyfriend, Joseph McEnroe. Mackenroe appeared quiet, intelligent, and reserved. He had worked various jobs but struggled financially. Friends rarely viewed him as openly violent. Yet investigators would later describe him as deeply influenced by grievance and bitterness. Together, Mikuel and Joseph formed a relationship that reinforced mutual resentment instead of stability. Each blamed others for their problems. Each believed they had been treated unfairly. Over time, detectives believe those shared frustrations transformed into a deadly partnership. During the first interviews after the murders, Miguel appeared emotional but controlled. She denied any involvement and expressed shock over the deaths. Joseph likewise denied knowledge of the crime. Their statements initially seemed cooperative, but detectives noticed inconsistencies. Timelines shifted. Small details failed to match. Certain explanations became increasingly difficult to verify. As investigators reconstructed the family's final hours, they learned that Miguel and Joseph had visited the Anderson home on Christmas Eve. Unlike an unknown intruder, they would not have needed to force entry. The family trusted them. That realization changed the entire direction of the investigation. Forensic teams carefully processed every room of the house. Ballistics evidence indicated multiple firearms had been used during the attack. Investigators concluded the killings had not occurred in a sudden emotional outburst, but as a systematic execution. Victims were murdered one after another. Some appeared to have been caught completely offguard. Others may have realized what was happening only seconds before their deaths. The most disturbing discovery involved the youngest victims. Olivia and Nathan had survived the initial shootings. Evidence suggested they remained alive after hearing gunfire inside the home. Instead of escaping, they were deliberately hunted through the house. Detectives later described this detail as one of the most heartbreaking aspects of the investigation. These were not accidental victims caught in crossfire. They became intentional targets despite being completely defenseless. Such decisions reflected extraordinary emotional detachment. Experienced homicide investigators, many of whom had spent decades examining violent crime, privately admitted that crimes involving entire families, were among the hardest to process. The murder of children, especially by someone they trusted, represented a level of betrayal that few cases ever reached. As evidence accumulated, financial records revealed another possible motive. Just weeks before Christmas, disagreements regarding money had intensified between Mikuel and her parents. Investigators uncovered evidence suggesting that Mikuel believed she had been unfairly denied financial assistance. There were disputes over housing, child support, and family obligations. While these disagreements alone could never explain six murders, detectives increasingly viewed them as part of a growing pattern of resentment that had reached a catastrophic breaking point. Meanwhile, Joseph Mackenrose's behavior after the killings attracted additional scrutiny. Rather than displaying genuine grief, investigators believed he focused on maintaining an appearance of normaly. Detectives later testified that both suspects behaved less like traumatized family members and more like individuals carefully attempting to distance themselves from suspicion. Then came the breakthrough. Digital evidence, witness timelines, forensic analysis, and inconsistencies during repeated interviews began aligning into a single narrative. Every major investigative path pointed back toward Mckela Anderson and Joseph McEnroe. The quiet Christmas gathering inside the Anderson home had not ended because of strangers. According to investigators, it had ended because two people the family loved had arrived carrying a plan that would erase three generations in a single night. By the final days of December 2007, detectives had reached a conclusion they had almost hoped would prove false. Every significant lead, every timeline, every interview, and every piece of forensic evidence continued to point toward the same two people. The massacre inside the Anderson home had not been committed by an unknown intruder. According to investigators, it had been planned by Michelle Anderson and her boyfriend Joseph McEnroe. On December 31, just one week after the murders, King County detectives moved in. SWAT officers surrounded the apartment where the couple had been staying. The arrest was carried out without gunfire, but the atmosphere was tense. Investigators knew they were dealing with suspects accused of eliminating an entire family, including two small children. Every movement was treated as a potential threat. Once inside separate interrogation rooms, detectives began the long process of confronting both suspects with the evidence. At first, neither admitted responsibility. Mikuel insisted she loved her family. Joseph denied any involvement beyond spending time with Michelle during the holidays. Both attempted to explain away inconsistencies in their movements, but experienced investigators had already compared their statements against witness accounts, physical evidence, and electronic records. The explanations simply did not fit. As forensic testing continued, prosecutors became increasingly confident they could reconstruct the entire sequence of events. According to investigators, Mikuel and Joseph arrived at the Anderson home on Christmas Eve, knowing exactly what they intended to do. The family welcomed them inside without hesitation. It was Christmas. They were relatives. No one expected danger. At some point during the evening, the violence began. Wayne Anderson became one of the first victims. Judy was murdered shortly afterward. Scott and Erica were then executed inside the home they believed was the safest place they could be. Finally came the most heartbreaking moments of the entire case. 5-year-old Olivia, 3-year-old Nathan, children too young to understand why their grandparents' home had suddenly become a place of terror. Investigators later stated that the evidence suggested the children were not accidental witnesses. They were deliberately killed to eliminate every surviving member of the household. For many detectives, this detail became impossible to forget. Murder investigations often expose humanity at its worst. But crimes involving entire families carry a different psychological weight. They erase generations in a matter of minutes. Holidays, birthdays, photographs, traditions, everything connected to that family stops at once. Incarnation. Six lives disappeared from the community in a single Christmas night. Preparing the case for trial proved enormously complicated. Prosecutors spent years organizing thousands of pages of evidence, forensic reports, witness interviews, crime scene photographs, and expert testimony. Defense attorneys challenged timelines, questioned aspects of the investigation, and argued that the state's reconstruction contained unanswered questions. The case moved slowly through Washington's court system. Year after year passed. Families of the victims continued waiting. Residents of Carnation continued remembering. The empty Anderson house became a painful reminder of what had happened there. For many people in the community, Christmas never felt the same again. When the trial finally began years later, the courtroom filled with investigators who had devoted countless hours to the case. Jurors were introduced to photographs of the crime scene, ballistic evidence, and testimony describing the final hours inside the Anderson home. Witness after witness painted the same picture, a family gathering, complete trust. then calculated violence. The prosecution argued that financial resentment had become the driving force behind the murders. According to their theory, Mcklly believed her parents had refused financial support she expected, creating years of bitterness that ultimately escalated into murder. Joseph McEnroe, prosecutors argued, shared those grievances and willingly participated in carrying out the plan. The defense rejected that interpretation. They questioned elements of the forensic timeline and attempted to undermine portions of the prosecution's narrative. But as testimony accumulated, jurors were presented with an increasingly detailed reconstruction supported by physical evidence and investigative findings. Perhaps the most emotional testimony came from relatives forced to describe the enormous void left behind. Wayne and Judy were remembered as devoted parents and grandparents. Scott was described as hard-working and deeply committed to his family. Erica was remembered for her kindness and dedication to her children. Olivia had only just begun elementary school. Nathan had barely begun life. Photographs shown in court captured birthdays, family vacations, Christmas mornings, ordinary smiles, moments that suddenly became the last surviving memories of people who would never create new ones. For jurors, those images transformed the victims from names in a case file into a real family whose future had been erased forever. After weeks of testimony, the jury reached its decision. Male Anderson was found guilty on multiple counts of aggravated first-degree murder. Joseph McEnroe was also convicted for his role in the massacre. The verdict brought a measure of legal closure, but it could never restore what had been lost inside that home on Christmas Eve. During sentencing, prosecutors described the crime as one of the most coldblooded family annihilations in Washington history. The judge agreed. Both defendants received life sentences without the possibility of parole. Neither would ever again walk free. Even after the convictions, investigators continued reflecting on the extraordinary betrayal at the center of the case. Unlike many notorious murders committed by strangers, this tragedy occurred because the victims opened their front door to people they loved. There were no masks, no forced entry, no desperate struggle to identify an unknown attacker. Trust itself became the weapon. The Carnation murders left lasting consequences far beyond one family. Law enforcement agencies studied the investigation as an example of how domestic grievances can evolve into carefully planned acts of extreme violence. Criminal psychologists pointed to the case as a reminder that resentment, financial desperation, and emotional isolation can combine into a dangerous mixture when reinforced between two people who continually validate each other's anger. For the residents of Carnation, however, academic explanations never mattered as much as personal memory. The Anderson family had been neighbors, friends, parents, grandparents, children whose laughter had once echoed through the same streets, now remembered only through photographs and memorials. Every December, the story returns. Christmas lights appear across Washington neighborhoods. Families gather around dinner tables. Children wait impatiently for morning presents. And somewhere in the memories of investigators, relatives, and longtime residents of Carnation, another house still stands frozen in time. A house where wrapped gifts remained beneath the Christmas tree, where dinner preparations were never finished, and where six members of the same family unknowingly celebrated their final Christmas together. The Carnation murders remain among the most disturbing crimes in Washington history. Not because they involved the largest number of victims or the longest investigation, but because they shattered one of society's deepest assumptions that home, family, and Christmas are places of safety. On the night of December 24th, 2007, that assumption died alongside six innocent people. And for Washington State, it became a reminder that sometimes the greatest danger is not the stranger outside the door, but the familiar face welcomed inside. Number three, Robert Lee Yates. The moment a single bullet casing was matched to a second crime scene in Spokane, the investigation pivoted from a series of possibly unrelated homicides to the pursuit of one man. But that match came late, terribly late. By then, Robert Lee Yates Jr. had already been killing for more than two decades, though the full scope of his violence would not be understood until long after he was in handcuffs. In the city of Spokane, where neighbors knew each other's names, and the pace of life moved slowly enough to notice an unfamiliar car, Yates operated in the open, shielded not by cleverness, but by the one thing no one could see past, his respectability. Born on May 27th, 1952 in the small town of Oak Harbor, Washington, Yates grew up in a family rooted in structure, faith, and military tradition. His father was a corrections officer. His mother was a homemaker who kept the household in order. Young Robert was a quiet, unremarkable student. He did not stand out academically. He did not stand out socially. He entered the US Army after high school and became a helicopter pilot. eventually rising to the rank of chief warrant officer 4. He served in operations overseas, earned commenations and was regarded by peers as a competent and professional aviator. He married Linda Brewer in 1975 and they eventually settled in Spokane where they raised five children. The family attended church. They lived on a treelined street in a modest but well-maintained home. Yates mowed his lawn, coached little league, and helped with neighborhood projects. The dissonance between this exterior and the acts he committed is not unusual in serial cases, but in Yates's case, it remained intact for an extraordinarily long time. His earliest confirmed killing dates to 1975. Yates later confessed to the murders of two young women, college students in Walaw Wala during that year. Their remains were found in a shallow grave, but the case remained cold for decades. There may have been additional killings during the late 1970s and 1980s, but the documentary evidence is thin and the confessions inconsistent. What is known with certainty is that beginning in 1996, Yates embarked on a concentrated series of murders in and around Spokane. His victims were overwhelmingly women engaged in sex work or struggling with drug addiction found in the neighborhoods along East Sprag Avenue, Spokane's equivalent of the Pacific Highway Southrip in King County. He would approach them in his white Corvette, a conspicuous car later traced by witnesses or occasionally in other vehicles. He would drive them to isolated locations, shoot them in the head, and bury or conceal their bodies. Some he left in open spaces, one he buried in his own yard. Between 1996 and 1998, Spokane experienced a surge in missing and murdered women that drew increasing media and law enforcement attention. The Spokane task force was established to address what appeared to be a serial pattern. Detectives canvased the corridor, interviewed sex workers, compiled license plates, and reviewed every connection between the victims. The investigation was painstaking, hampered by limited forensic technology and the transient nature of many victims lifestyles, which made establishing clear timelines difficult. Yates came to the attention of investigators in 1999 after a surviving witness reported being picked up by a man in a white Corvette. A check of vehicle registration records identified Yates as the owner. When detectives ran his name, they discovered he had previously been questioned in connection with one of the earlier missing women. A deeper look revealed his proximity to multiple crime scenes. Fibers from his vehicle matched evidence collected from victims. And in a pivotal development, a 0.25 caliber handgun belonging to Yates was ballistically linked to bullets recovered from several of the dead women. He was arrested on April 18th, 2000 at his home on South 51st Avenue in Spokane. Linda Yates and the children were present. Neighbors gathered on the sidewalk. No one believed it. The cognitive gap between the man they had known and the crimes being described was for many simply unbridgegable. One neighbor told reporters that Yates had been at a barbecue the previous weekend. Another described him as the nicest man on the street. In 2000, Yates pleaded guilty to 13 counts of firstdegree murder in Spokane County and received a sentence of 408 years without parole. But the legal proceedings did not end. there. In 2002, he was extradited to Pierce County to face charges for two additional murders from the 1970s. One of those victims had been just barely out of her teenage years. In Pierce County, Yates was sentenced to death. He has since exhausted multiple rounds of appeals and remains on death row at the Washington State Penitentiary in Walaw Wala. The Yates case forced Spokane to confront an uncomfortable truth that serial violence had been unfolding for years within its borders, targeting a population whose disappearances did not always prompt immediate alarm. It also underscored how thoroughly the architecture of trust, military service, fatherhood, churchgoing, community involvement could be leveraged as camouflage. Yates was not a drifter. He was not a recluse. He was the man on the other side of the fence waving as he walked to his car. And for more than 20 years, that was enough. Number four, Wesley Allen. The sequence of events that led to the capture of Wesley Allen unfolded in under 3 minutes at a movie theater in Cas, Washington. On November 13th, 1989, Dodd attempted to abduct a young boy from the restroom of the New Liberty Theater. The child screamed. A nearby patron intervened. Dodd ran. He was caught in the parking lot by a civilian who held him until police arrived. And yet, the speed of his apprehension belied the depth of what was about to be uncovered. Inside his apartment, investigators found a diary, hundreds of pages, handwritten, cataloging fantasies, plans, and meticulous records of crimes already committed. What had seemed like a failed abduction attempt was in reality the exposure of one of the most methodically documented predatory histories in the Pacific Northwest. Dodd was born on July 3rd, 1961 in Tapenish, Washington. His parents divorced when he was young and the home environment by his own later description was emotionally cold. He described his father as distant and his mother as uninvolved. There was no documented physical abuse, no obvious catalytic trauma of the kind that surfaces in many serial offender backgrounds. What there was instead was isolation. Dodd was left alone frequently, supervised rarely, and developed deviant sexual fixations at an extraordinarily young age. By 13, he was exposing himself to children in his neighborhood. By 15, he had escalated to physical contact offenses. He was caught multiple times as a juvenile and a young adult, arrested on molestation related charges, and cycled through brief interventions, none of which involved meaningful psychological treatment or long-term supervision. He served short sentences, attended minimal counseling, and was released into the community each time with no substantive monitoring. His military service, a brief stint in the Navy from which he was discharged, followed the same pattern of transient, lowimpact consequence for predatory behavior. He offended on base, was investigated, and was separated from service. He returned to Washington State. Dodd settled in the Vancouver, Washington area in the late 1980s and took a job at a shipping warehouse. He lived alone. He was unremarkable to co-workers, punctual, quiet, steady. Outside of work, his life was consumed by planning. His diaries, recovered after his arrest, described a progression from fantasy to preparation to execution, with a level of organizational detail that disturbed even veteran investigators. He listed materials needed. He mapped locations. He recorded timets. He wrote about target criteria. The diaries were not the ravings of a disorganized mind. They were structured, coherent, and goaloriented. On September 4th, 1989, Dodd attacked two brothers, ages 10 and 11, at David Douglas Park in Vancouver. He lured them into an isolated section of the park, assaulted them, and fatally stabbed both. The boys were found by a search party later that evening. The community was devastated. The investigation initially focused on known offenders in the area and Dodd, whose juvenile and adult records were incomplete and scattered across multiple jurisdictions, did not immediately surface as a suspect. Less than 2 months later, on October 29th, Dodd abducted a 4-year-old boy from a playground at Richmond Elementary School in Vancouver. He took the child to his apartment where the boy was held captive overnight. The details of what occurred during that period are documented in Dodd's own diary and in the forensic findings. The child was murdered the following morning. Dodd photographed parts of the process. He then placed the body in the trunk of his car and drove to a lake where he disposed of it. His arrest at the CAM's theater 2 weeks later was not the result of forensic linkage or investigative pressure. It was an act of impulsive compulsion. He could not stop and a brave intervention by a stranger. Once in custody, Dodd confessed fully without equivocation. He waved his right to trial and entered a guilty plea. He was sentenced to death. On January 5th, 1993, Wesley Allen Dodd was executed by hanging at the Washington State Penitentiary, the first legal hanging in the United States in nearly three decades. He had specifically requested this method, and the legal proceedings to honor that request generated significant public debate. In his final statement, he expressed no ambiguity about his own dangerousness. He told interviewers and prison officials that if released, he would kill again. He said it without hesitation. And in a statement that would be cited in criminal psychology textbooks for years afterward, he said that the death penalty was the only measure that could guarantee prevention, not because he wanted to die, but because he knew with clinical certainty, that nothing else would stop him. The Dodd case became a landmark in how law enforcement agencies approached the tracking and monitoring of serial child predators. His repeated encounters with the justice system, arrests, short sentences, minimal therapy, no cross-jurisdictional tracking, laid bare the systemic failures that had allowed him to escalate from exposure to assault to murder over the course of 15 years. Washington state subsequently reformed its sex offender registration and notification protocols, contributing to the national push that eventually produced Megan's law and subsequent federal legislation. Dodd did not create these laws alone, but his case and his diaries provided the kind of harrowing evidence that made legislative inaction politically impossible. Number five, Jake Bird. The arrests of Jake Bird required the response of several officers in the early hours of October 30th, 1947 after neighbors in a residential section of Tacoma heard screaming from inside the home of Bertha Klut. When police arrived, they found Clute and her 17-year-old daughter, Beverly June, both fatally wounded from an ax attack. Bird was caught fleeing the scene, still carrying the weapon. He resisted arrest violently, injuring two officers before being subdued. What appeared at that point to be a single incident of breaking and entering turned homicidal, a terrible but contained event, would within months expand into something much larger. Jake Bird was not a desperate burglar who panicked. He was a man who had been moving across the United States for decades, leaving bodies behind him in towns that had never thought to compare notes. Bird was born in 1901 in Louisiana. His early life is poorly documented. What is known places him in a string of transient labor jobs, railroad work, migrant farming, manual labor that carried him through the Midwest, the South, and eventually the Pacific Northwest. He traveled by freight train. He had no permanent address. He appeared and disappeared from communities with no trace. And in the era before centralized criminal databases or interstate forensic communication, his movement was effectively untraceable. At trial in Tacoma, Bird was convicted of the firstdegree murders of Bertha and Beverly June Klut. The proceedings drew attention not only for the brutality of the crime, but for Bird's courtroom demeanor. After receiving his death sentence, he addressed the court in a statement that has become one of the most unusual episodes in Washington legal history. He declared what he called a hex, a curse on those involved in his prosecution, stating that people connected to his trial would die before he did. Within the following months, the judge who sentenced him and one of the attorneys involved in the case both died. A third person associated with the trial also died within the year. The coincidences generated sensational media coverage and public speculation, though there is no credible evidence of any causal connection. While on death row, Bird was interviewed by investigators from multiple states. Through a combination of his own admissions and subsequent law enforcement re-examination of unsolved cases, Bird was linked to as many as 44 murders across the country, stretching from the 1930s through the 1940s. The confirmed connections are fewer. Investigators in Ohio, Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, Michigan, Wisconsin, Utah, Illinois, and Florida all identified potential matches involving ax attacks on women, break-ins that escalated to homicide, and transient suspect descriptions that aligned with Bird's physical characteristics and travel patterns. Confirmation at the forensic level was impossible for most of these cases, given the technology of the era. Bird was executed by hanging at the Washington State Penitentiary on July 15th, 1949. He maintained his hex to the end and expressed no remorse for the Tacoma killings. His case represents one of the earliest recognized examples of a mobile serial killer exploiting the pre-digital gaps in American law enforcement. the absence of national communication networks, the lack of fingerprint databases accessible across jurisdictions, and the social invisibility of migrant labor workers all converge to make Jake Bird functionally invisible for most of his life. He passed through America like weather, and behind him, cases went cold with no one aware they were connected to the same man. Number six, Joseph Condro. The disappearance of 8-year-old Reema Traxxler in August 1985 from Long View, Washington, provoked a community search, a police investigation, and eventually a long, slow silence. She vanished from the street where she lived. There were no witnesses. There were no suspects. Years passed and the case settled into the particular kind of grief that small towns absorb when a child goes missing and no answers come. What no one knew, not the investigators, not the family, not the neighbors, was that the man responsible lived within walking distance of the Traxxler home. He had offered to help with the search. He had been questioned briefly and released and he had continued to live his life for the next 13 years waiting in a sense for the science to catch up. Joseph Edward Condro was born and raised in the Long View Keelso area of southwestern Washington. He was known in the neighborhood as a familiar somewhat rough but not alarming figure. He had a criminal record, minor offenses, no prior violence that had drawn significant attention. He drank. He worked intermittent jobs. He socialized with neighbors, attended community events, and was familiar to the families on the street. In the vocabulary of true crime, he was a known quantity, someone whose presence was unremarkable, precisely because he had always been there. In 1996, 12-year-old Cara Rudd went missing in Long View. Her body was found in the Cowitz River. The cause of death was drowning, complicated by evidence of sexual assault. Investigators struggled with the case. There was limited physical evidence and the circumstances made it difficult to differentiate foul play from accident during the initial stages of recovery. Condro was not initially a primary suspect. The breakthrough came in 1998 and 1999 as DNA technology improved and investigators re-examined both the Traxxler and RUD cases with fresh forensic tools. Genetic material recovered from the Rudd crime scene was matched to Condro. He was arrested and under interrogation confessed first to the killing of Cara Ruddd then to the murder of Reema Traxler more than a decade earlier. He led police to the site where he had concealed Reema's remains. They were found in a rural area outside of Long View, buried in a location that had been less than a mile from ongoing search efforts in 1985. Condro was charged with aggravated first-degree murder. In 2002, he was found dead in his cell at the Cowitz County Jail. He had taken his own life before his case could proceed to trial. His death foreclosed both the possibility of further confessions and the legal closure that the families had sought for years. The impact on Long View was profound. Condro had not been an outsider. He had been a neighbor. He had been present during the grief, present during the searching, and present during the community meetings that followed each disappearance. The realization that predation could originate from within the most intimate circles of a small town forced a reckoning with assumptions about safety and proximity. It also underscored the degree to which forensic science, when it finally arrives, can collapse decades of silence in a single laboratory result. DNA did not just solve the condro case. It ended a lie that had been maintained by geography, familiarity, and the passage of time. Number seven, Warren Forest. For decades, Warren Leslie Forest moved through Spokane's social infrastructure as a figure of trust. He was a music teacher. He led church choirs. He worked with children and families. He was respected in the circles that mattered, education, worship, community service. And from within that architecture of social credibility, he committed acts that would not be prosecuted until the mid 1990s. Long after the damage had compounded beyond recovery. Forest was born in 1938 and raised in the Spokane area. He pursued education, earned teaching credentials, and entered the school system as a music instructor. He married. He had children. From the outside, his life followed the most stable, most legible trajectory available to a man in mid-century Washington. But behind this surface, Forest was a predator whose crime stretched across decades and involved sexual assault, manipulation, and eventually murder. In the 1970s, women in the Spokane area began to go missing under circumstances that defied easy explanation. Some were associated with social margins, hitchhiking, transient living, economic instability. Others were connected to forest through acquaintance or social circles. One of his victims, a young woman he was sexually involved with, disappeared in 1974. Her remains were not found until years later. Forest was not considered a suspect at the time. His public reputation was too solid, too embedded in the community's trust. The investigation that eventually led to Forest's arrest was not the result of a single forensic breakthrough. It was the product of cumulative suspicion, cold case re-examination, and the testimony of surviving witnesses who had endured his abuse and finally found the institutional support to come forward. In 1994, Forest was charged with first-degree murder for the death of the young woman who had disappeared two decades prior. The trial revealed a pattern of sexual coercion, control, and violence that had been concealed behind his professional identity. Forest was convicted and sentenced to life in prison. He died in custody. His case remains one of the clearest examples of how institutional trust conferred by profession, religion, and community standing can be weaponized to create a zone of impunity that persists for extraordinary lengths of time. Number eight, Israel Keys. On the evening of February of 2012, an 18-year-old barista closed up a coffee stand in Anchorage, Alaska, and was never seen alive again. The abduction of Samantha Koig and the subsequent investigation that led to the arrest of Israel Keys in Texas two months later is the case most publicly associated with his name. But Keys's connection to Washington State runs deeper than most summaries acknowledge. He had lived in the Pacific Northwest. He had buried supplies in Washington, and at least one confirmed homicide in his history is tied to the state, part of a pattern of premeditated geographically distributed violence that made Keys unlike almost any other serial offender in modern American criminal history. Israel Keys was born on January 7th, 1978, and raised in a large family with ties to fundamentalist religious communities. The family moved frequently during his childhood from Utah to Washington to Oregon and elsewhere, living at various times in remote offrid conditions. Keys later described an upbringing defined by isolation, strict religious control, and a growing internal disconnect. He was intelligent, capable with his hands, and socially adept enough to pass unnoticed in most settings. He joined the army, served at Fort Lewis in Washington State, and received an honorable discharge. He became a licensed contractor in Anchorage. He had a daughter, he maintained relationships, and simultaneously he planned and carried out murders across the country with a discipline that remains almost without parallel. Keys's methodology was defined by preparation and geographic disconnection. He would fly or drive hundreds or thousands of miles from his home base, retrieve pre-buried kill kits containing weapons, cash, and tools, and commit crimes in areas where he had no personal ties. He explicitly avoided selecting victims he knew. He chose targets at random. He studied forensic countermeasures. He avoided digital footprints. He paid in cash. He disabled his cell phone during travel. He knew what investigators looked for and he engineered his behavior to leave nothing behind. His confirmed victims include a couple murdered in Vermont in 2011, Bill and Lorraine Courier, a crime he later confessed to after his arrest. He was linked to Washington through travel records, cashed supplies, and his own admissions during interrogation. He alluded to additional killings, but refused to provide full details, maintaining a degree of control over the narrative, even from inside a jail cell. The investigation into keys unraveled rapidly after the Kuwinig abduction. He had used Kunig's debit card after her death, activating it in Texas. FBI agents tracked the withdrawals and arrested him during a traffic stop in Lufkin, Texas. In custody, Keys entered into protracted debriefing sessions with the FBI, providing limited confessions while withholding names and dates. He described his crimes with an unsettling calm. He discussed logistics. He described pleasures. He described the waiting. On December 2nd, 2012, Israel Keys was found dead in his cell at the Anchorage Correctional Complex. He had taken his own life. He left behind a long handwritten note and a drawing rendered in his own blood. The FBI's investigation into his full criminal history remains open. Multiple unsolved cases across the United States in Washington, Oregon, New York, and elsewhere continue to be examined for potential connections. His refusal to fully confess means the complete scope of his violence may never be known. Keys represents a category of offender that law enforcement had long theorized but rarely encountered in documented form. The methodical, mobile, forensically aware killer who selects victims with no connection to himself, crosses state lines routinely and leaves virtually no trace. His ties to Washington through military service, residence, and cashed supplies place the state squarely within his operational geography. And the fact that his buried kits remained undetected for years, waiting in forest floors and rural lots, means that parts of Washington may still hold physical evidence of his planning that has never been recovered. Number nine, Kenneth Bianke. The morning of January 12th, 1979 began with the discovery of two bodies in the backseat of a car parked on a residential culde-sac in Bellingham, Washington. The victims were Karen Mandic and Diane Wilder, both students at Western Washington University. They had been strangled. The car had been parked deliberately, almost arranged, in a location that suggested the killer intended the bodies to be found. Within days, the trail led back to a man who had recently moved to Bellingham from Los Angeles, a man who had applied to join the Bellingham Police Department, and a man whose name, once cross referenced with law enforcement contacts in California, triggered a cascade that would finally close the Hillside Strangler case. Kenneth Allesio Bianke was born on May 22nd, 1951 in Rochester, New York. His biological mother was a sex worker who gave him up for adoption shortly after birth. He was adopted by Francis and Nicholas Bianke, a workingclass couple who provided a stable, if emotionally rigid, home. Francis, by multiple accounts, was overprotective, anxious, and controlling, traits that deepened Kenneth's social dysfunction rather than correcting it. As a child and teenager, Bianke was a compulsive liar. He fabricated stories about his background, his accomplishments, and his relationships with a fluency that went beyond ordinary adolescent exaggeration. He was diagnosed with passive aggressive personality disorder during a childhood evaluation, and his academic and social trajectory was marked by underperformance, manipulation, and an inability to sustain relationships that required genuine emotional reciprocity. In the early 1970s, Bianke relocated to Los Angeles, where he reconnected with his cousin, Angelo Buono, Junior Buono, was older, more dominant, and deeply violent. The pair formed a predatory partnership that between October 1977 and February 1978, terrorized the hills above Los Angeles. Over the course of roughly four months, they abducted, sexually assaulted, and murdered 10 young women and girls, ranging in age from 12 to 28. The killings became known as the Hillside Strangler murders, initially attributed to a single perpetrator, and the investigation consumed the Los Angeles Police Department and generated national headlines. When the murders stopped in early 1978, investigators assumed the killer had either died, been imprisoned for another crime, or fled the area. In fact, the partnership had dissolved. [clears throat] Bianke had moved north, relocating to Bellingham, Washington, where he attempted to construct a new identity. He found work as a security guard. He applied to the police department. He presented himself as a responsible young man, starting fresh. And for nearly a year, the pose held. The Bellingham murders were his undoing. Unlike the Los Angeles killings, which had been committed in partnership with the more experienced Buono, the Mandic and Wilder homicides were Bianke's solo work, and they were sloppy. He had used his job as a security guard to lure the women, asking them to housesit a property he was ostensibly guarding, and the paper trail connecting him to the victims was thin but traceable. His car was seen near the location. His behavior in the days following the murders was erratic enough to draw co-worker attention. And critically, when Bellingham detectives contact LAPD about the suspect, the name triggered an immediate connection to the stalled hillside strangler investigation. Bianke was arrested in Bellingham on January 12th, 1979. What followed was one of the most controversial legal and psychological proceedings of the decade. Bianke attempted to claim insanity, presenting an alter ego named Steve Walker, who had purportedly committed the crimes. Multiple psychiatrists evaluated him. Some initially believed the dissociative identity claim. Others, including Dr. Martin Or demonstrated through careful testing that Bianke was faking, the multiple personality defense collapsed. Bianke eventually agreed to a plea deal testifying against his cousin Angelo Buono in exchange for avoiding the death penalty. He received a sentence of life without parole in Washington state and additional concurrent life sentences in California. Bianke remains incarcerated. He has been denied parole multiple times. The Bellingham chapter of the Hillside Strangler case is often treated as a footnote to the Los Angeles killings, but it deserves independent weight. It was in Washington that Bianke was forced to act alone, and it was that solitary action stripped of Buono's direction and discipline that produced the errors which ended both their criminal lives. Bellingham was not where the hillside strangler was born. It was where he was finally irrevocably exposed. Number 10, Mitchell RP. On the afternoon of November 27th, 1981, the day after Thanksgiving, a man walked into the Pacific First Federal Savings Bank in Olympia, Washington, with a 38 caliber revolver and a plan that disintegrated almost immediately. Mitchell Edward RP intended to rob the bank. That much proceeded as planned. He gained control of the tellers, collected cash, and prepared to leave. Then two bank employees moved or spoke in a way that triggered a response no one in the room anticipated. Rupe shot both women in the head, killing them instantly. He walked out of the bank, was identified within hours through witness descriptions, and was arrested the same day. The robbery netted less than $30,000. Two people were dead and what should have been a straightforward capital murder prosecution became one of the strangest death penalty cases in Washington state history. RP was born in 1954 and raised in the Olympia area. His background was marked by petty criminal activity, inconsistent employment, and substance use. He had prior arrests. He was not a sophisticated criminal. The bank robbery itself was poorly planned, poorly executed, and reliant on a level of impulse control that RP did not possess. The decision to shoot the two tellers, Candace Hemsley and Winifred Petty, appears to have been reactive rather than premeditated, though the legal proceedings would debate that distinction at length. He was tried, convicted of two counts of aggravated first-degree murder, and sentenced to death. The conviction and sentencing were straightforward, but the execution was not. Over the following years, RP's weight increased dramatically during his incarceration. By the time his execution date approached, he weighed more than 400 lb. His legal team argued that hanging, the method of execution available in Washington at the time, posed a risk of decapitation given his body weight and that this would constitute cruel and unusual punishment. The argument went to the Washington State Supreme Court, which ruled in 1994 that hanging RP would indeed be unconstitutional under the circumstances. The ruling did not vacate his sentence, but it effectively suspended its execution. The case entered legal limbo. RP spent more than two decades on death row. While his legal status was debated, he filed appeals. He resisted reclassification. The state of Washington later adopted lethal injection as an alternative method, but subsequent rulings and procedural questions prevented the sentence from being carried out. RP died in prison on February 9th, 2006 of liver disease. He was 52 years old. He never faced execution. The RUP case, while not as expansive in scope or victim count as the other entries in this ranking, occupies a distinct place in Washington criminal history. It forced the state to confront the practical, constitutional, and medical complications of capital punishment in ways that no prior case had required. It also stands as a grim reminder of how a single act of impulsive violence, 30 seconds inside a bank, two gunshots, can generate legal reverberations that outlast the perpetrator himself.
